newsitem.title: USA: US Democrats want probe of Republican fund-raising.
newsitem.headline: US Democrats want probe of Republican fund-raising.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
Democrats on Friday demanded that two congressional committees investigating alleged campaign finance misdeeds subpoena more documents relating to Republican Party fund raising.

Ohio Sen. John Glenn, the ranking Democrat on the Senate committee probing the affair, said in a statement it was "imperative that the Governmental Affairs Committee issue subpoenas to all parties involved in this matter."

The demand, in a letter to committee chairman Sen. Fred Thompson of Tennessee, came a day after the Republicans said they had returned $122,000 in political contributions because it learned the money came from the Hong Kong parent company of a Florida-based subsidiary.

Thompson agreed to issue six subpoenas relating to Republican fund-raising activities but turned down Democratic requests for an additional six subpoenas, including one for the papers of former Republican Party chairman Haley Barbour.
The exact scope and wording of the subpoenas is yet to be worked out.
"Any delay in issuing subpoenas will only hamper our efforts to get to the bottom of this situation," Glenn said.

Representative Henry Waxman, the ranking Democrat on the House government reform and oversight committee, said committee chairman Dan Burton of Indiana was ignoring Democratic requests for an even-handed investigation.
"I am deeply disappointed that you have not even given the minority the courtesy of acknowledging our request," Waxman said in a letter to Burton.
All the Democrats on the committee sent a letter to Attorney General Janet Reno asking her to investigate.

The donations returned by the Republicans were made between 1991 and 1993 by Young Brothers Development. In 1994, the same company also guaranteed a $2.2 million loan to a Republican Party think-tank, the National Policy Forum, established by Barbour.

Congressional sources said Young Brothers appeared to be a shell company controlled by Ambrous Tung Young, a Hong Kong businessman. The company's sole U.S. asset was an apartment in Georgetown, an exclusive Washington neighbourhood.

Media reports said the money went straight into Republican Party coffers. In 1996, the bank that loaned the money called the loan, Barbour refused to pay the whole amount and Young was forced to pay $500,000.

Meanwhile, congressional sources said an investigation team including at least two FBI agents would soon leave Washington for Asia in an effort to track down and interview key witnesses suspected of illegally providing the Democratic Party with foreign money.
Several key figures in the scandal have fled to Asia and are thought to be unlikely to cooperate with the probe.
Senate hearings are expected to begin in early July, with House hearings beginning in the fall.
